prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles for the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are a physical-chemical solution to a specific molecular problem: a lipid whose headgroup is cationic at low pH, so it complexes and encapsulates nucleic acid, but near-neutral at physiological pH, so it is tolerated in circulation, and which promotes non-bilayer, fusogenic phase behaviour once protonated in the endosome. That is lipid self-assembly, charge regulation and membrane phase behaviour used as a design principle, and it is exactly the kind of reduction of a complicated biological barrier to general thermodynamic concepts that I think Chemistry should reward. The consequence is independently verified at scale: an approved siRNA drug and billions of mRNA vaccine doses. The 2023 Medicine prize honoured nucleoside modification, not the vehicle, so the delivery chemistry remains unrecognised.
statement.case_against: Credit is spread across at least six names (Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson, Langer), the three-person cap forces an unavoidable exclusion, and the priority record for the ionizable lipid itself versus the formulation process is contested. Support in the opening round is also narrow (four of eight rank it, and Linke placed it eighth), whereas base editing and protein degradation each drew broad top-three support. A reasonable colleague can argue that this is formulation and pharmaceutical engineering built on an earlier Medicine prize, and that I rank it first partly because it sits close to my own field.

responses.point: Linke ranked base editing first and placed ionizable lipid nanoparticles last on his list, while giving phase separation (B047) a respectable fourth place; his view of B013 appears to be that the physical chemistry is less central than the clinical story.
responses.response: I disagree with the characterisation of the lipid work as mainly application. The central insight is a physical-chemical one: pKa-tuned charge, and the shift from bilayer to inverted non-bilayer phases that allows endosomal escape. This came from phase-behaviour studies of lipid mixtures before it became a drug, which is why I treat it as a concept and not merely a formulation. I do accept his point that base editing has the cleaner, more compact attribution, and I would not be unhappy to see it recognised, but I do not accept that a clearer attribution makes it the better science.

responses.point: Aili ranks base editing first with the Liu-Komor-Gaudelli trio and places lipid nanoparticles third, arguing that delivery remains unrecognised and has enormous societal impact, while noting that credit among six names is difficult.
responses.response: I agree with Aili that delivery is unrecognised and that the mechanism is chemistry-centred, and I welcome that support. Where I differ is on the trio for B024. I put Liu alone in my opening ballot because Komor and Gaudelli were lead trainees in a Liu-directed programme, and I would like the committee to say explicitly why a first-author postdoc is a laureate here when we would not normally default to that for a PI-led programme. If the committee wants a three-person base-editing prize I can live with it, but it should be argued and not assumed.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks PROTACs and molecular glues first as a new chemical modality built on induced proximity, accepting that clinical approvals are still pending and that he relies on recalled priority.
responses.response: I find the induced-proximity concept persuasive and ranked it fourth for that reason, but I think his own maturity caveat carries more weight than his ranking allows. With no approved PROTAC of broad impact, the glue branch (thalidomide-cereblon, Handa) is on firmer ground than the PROTAC branch (Crews, Deshaies), and a combined configuration would blur two different stories. By comparison, lipid nanoparticles have already delivered approved drugs and vaccines. I would still treat PROTACs as a strong candidate in a few years, not as the obvious choice this year.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase first and phase separation seventh, saying the interpretation of condensates is not stable and that mature structure-plus-mechanism work should be rewarded.
responses.response: His scepticism about B047 is fair and it is why I list it only as an alternative and not as my preferred choice: the in vivo evidence for genuinely liquid-like assemblies, and the functional significance of the term, are still debated. I would qualify that the in vitro phase-diagram and multivalency physics is sound and well replicated, so the concern is about cellular interpretation, not the chemistry. I am sympathetic to a mature structural-mechanistic prize, but nitrogenase was supported by one member only, and I would like to hear whether the catalytic mechanism is settled enough to write a clean citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can agree on an allocation among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and which of the ionizable-lipid design and the formulation process carries priority.
Whether a Chemistry prize on lipid nanoparticles is seen as derivative of the 2023 Medicine prize.
Whether Komor and Gaudelli should share a base-editing prize with Liu, or whether Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID precedent changes the picture.
Whether the condensate field is stable enough in its in vivo interpretation for recognition now.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional connection to any candidate on the shortlist is apparent from my profile. I sit on the committee with Lund colleagues Linke and Somfai, which is not a candidate conflict. My research field (lipid self-assembly, membrane phase behaviour, and lipid-protein co-assembly in amyloid) is close to B013 and B047, so I flag this scientific proximity to the committee and welcome challenge to my ranking of those candidates.
